newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Latam stocks seen volatile on domestic concerns.
newsitem.headline: Latam stocks seen volatile on domestic concerns.

text.p: Latin American stock markets were expected to be volatile this week with investors turning their attention away from regional and U.S. issues to focus on concerns closer to home, analysts said.
Company results in Argentina, a fresh round of legislative sessions in Brasilia and labor unrest in Venezuela have investors carefully eyeing developments and taking cautious positions.

Mexican stocks, meanwhile, will continue to track U.S. long-bond prices, and the Chilean market will likely extend a rally last week that followed news of a major deal in the electricity sector, brokers said.
Brazilian stock volatility was expected with the resumption of legislative sessions and the approach of futures and options expirations on August 13 and 18, respectively.
"The market will once again begin to focus on Brasilia, where the Congress will initiate the second-half legislative period," one analyst said.

Prices early in the week will continue to feel the weight of any declines in U.S. stocks and concerns over the possibility of a wide July trade gap. Those factors caused the Sao Paulo bourse to plummet Friday, analysts said.
The bolsa's Bovespa index of 47 most-traded shares dropped 4.76 percent on Friday to 12,259 points on moderate volume of 823 million reais ($760 million).
Argentine stocks were expected to extend a pullback early in the week but level out quickly as the focus turned to company results, dealers said.
Traders said Friday's losses, linked to the surge in U.S. payrolls, were part of a healthy regrouping.
"This drop is not happening with a strong volume of sales but rather with low demand, which means the underlying trend remains positive," said Augusto Milou at brokers Galicia Valores.
The blue-chip MerVal index shed 1.1 percent to 841.08 Friday, wiping out gains to close flat on the week.
Mexican stocks were expected to zigzag through the week with higher U.S. long bond yields prompting investors to take profits after recent record-breaking gains, analysts said.

The bourse broke records last week as international fund managers scrambled to buy Mexican assets, pushing the blue-chip IPC index up 344.61 points, or 7.3 percent, to close at 5,067.03 points on Friday.
Stockwatchers said the bourse had shown resilience after a heady month that included landmark midterm elections, fallout from volatility in Brazil and second-quarter earnings.
They said they would track developments in the U.S. bond market to check whether higher yields would choke recent heavy liquidity flows into popular emerging markets venues.

Electricity stocks, which account for a 40 percent weighting in the blue-chip IPSA index, rallied Friday after the announcement of the deal, the largest investment by a foreign company in Chile's energy sector. The IPSA index ended the week up 1.17 percent at 135.69 points.
Individual stocks could also react next week to company conference calls and analysts' reports on second-quarter earnings released this week, traders said.

Venezuelan stocks could show further losses amid worries about the country's recent labor unrest, with a 12-hour national strike planned for August 6 to press for salary increases in the private sector.
The market's 19-share IBC index slipped 2.9 percent in thin trade last week amid concerns about the strike threat and the effects of a 27 percent increase in gasoline price.
((-- Paul Hughes, Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
